doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

chapter: Composing and the Thad Jones band
title: Compositions: the ballet and Quest Sonata
summary: The ballet 'My Name Is Jasmine But They Call Me Jazz' and a Library of Congress sonata; difficulty of notating jazz.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Have these kinds of experiences found their way into inspiration for compositions for you?

Oh yes, of course. I wrote a ballet more than ten years ago now, that was commissioned by a company in Columbus, Ohio, and the ballet is called “My Name Is Jasmine But They Call Me Jazz.” And it was played about five or six times. The ballet had to stay in their control for five years, and we have it now. We haven’t been able to produce it because it’s a big thing to produce a ballet but we have it back now. But I have recorded some of the songs. At that time, when I did it I couldn’t record any of the songs because they belonged to them. And I’ve also written for the Library of Congress a sonata called “Quest Sonata” that uses elements of African-American music, not necessarily jazz, but elements of African American music. But you would have to know that, because the interpretation of the player makes a difference. If I play it you’d definitely hear jazz. But if someone else reads it and they play it they would play it like a classic player.
There you go. Trying to get something on the page.

Yeah. It’s very hard to do, which is why jazz itself, we were able to continue keeping it because people got it from the record, not from the written page. Although you have jazz bands and they play jazz and they read music, it’s because of the band leader being able to instill the jazz inflection to that music. But if you don’t have the right people you’re not going to get that music. It takes a long time.
